docs.title: voles
docs.text:
Collocation-method solvers for Volterra integral and integro-differential equations (VIEs/VIDEs), based on:

Brunner H. Collocation Methods for Volterra Integral and Related Functional Differential Equations. Cambridge University Press; 2004.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
Equation Solver \(g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) solve_vie1 \(y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) solve_vie2 \(y'(t) = a(t)y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) solve_vide

Each takes its inputs either as arrays of samples on a uniform grid (dt=), the fastest path for sampled data, or as callables on a mesh you choose (mesh=), which also handles weakly singular kernels. Both return a VolterraSolution. The rules are on the Conventions page.

For a kernel \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\), optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=..., t_end=..., n_intervals=..., order=...) builds a Brunner-graded mesh, and declaring the exponent with kernel_singularity={0.0: alpha} switches the singular blocks to deterministic Gauss–Jacobi quadrature, typically 3–10× faster than declaring only the location. Collocation nodes for callable inputs can be given via coll_nodes, with gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes and lobatto_nodes for the classical families.

Upgrading from 0.10? See Migration from 0.10.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install voles[full]

This gives you the fully-capable package, so everything just works out of the box. Pre-built wheels are provided for Linux x86_64, macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon), and Windows x64. The D extension is bundled in the wheel and requires no extra tooling. Intel Macs are no longer supported as of 0.3.2; users can pin to volterra-equation-solvers==0.3.1 or build from source (see CONTRIBUTING.md).

Requirements: Python ≥ 3.10, numpy, scipy

If you have trouble installing a dependency, you can use a slimmer install instead. numba and scipy are only needed for some features (see below), so any of these will still give you a working package:

pip install voles          # core: numpy + scipy (no numba)
pip install voles --no-deps && pip install numpy   # leanest: numpy only, no scipy or numba

What the optional pieces buy you: - scipy (core dependency) — required for callable inputs and for VolterraSolution.to_ppoly(). - numba (added by [full]) — only needed for sampled inputs with quadrature="collocation" and a collocation setting not compiled into the D extension; the default product quadrature needs neither.

To build from source (e.g. on an unsupported platform), see CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Mathematical derivations
docs.text:
The docs/ directory contains worked derivations of the analytic solutions used in the test suite:

File Contents scalar_solutions.pdf Derivations for all six scalar test cases (VIE-1, VIE-2, VIDE) coupled_vector_solutions.pdf Derivations for the coupled 2×2 vector test cases, constructed via a similarity transform

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import voles

# y(t) = sin(t) satisfies this VIE-2
dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(0, 9.05, dt)
g = np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=g, dt=dt)
print(sol.y[:3], sol(0.123))

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Mean wall-clock execution time, measured on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-22.04 runner (2-core x86_64 VM on an Intel Xeon 8370C, 2.8 GHz base / 3.5 GHz boost). Mean time is averaged over a variable number of calibrated rounds (from ~3 for large inputs up to ~6000 for small inputs). A dash (—) marks sizes a row is not benchmarked at (to keep the CI job fast). The timings are for warm calls: the first solve in a process that needs scipy's quadrature (callable inputs with a declared singularity) also imports it, about half a second once.

These tables are regenerated automatically by the benchmark CI job on pushes to main that touch code (docs-only pushes are skipped), and this page is redeployed with the fresh numbers. An interactive history of the same measurements is published at the benchmark dashboard.

For the asymptotic complexity (which is what stays fixed as the implementation evolves), see the Benchmarks section of the README.

docs.title: Sampled inputs
docs.text:
Mean time in milliseconds with sampled inputs (arrays, dt=), by input length \(N\) (number of samples). These rows use quadrature="collocation", the compiled path:

Notes on the rows:

  • VIE-1 with continuous=True is not shown separately: its timings are indistinguishable from the default (discontinuous) VIE-1 rows.
  • d=8 is the largest compile-time-specialized dimension in the D extension; d=16 exercises the runtime-dimension path (LAPACK, or the pure-D LU fallback used on the CI runner). Cost grows as \(d^2\) either way.
  • Numba fallback: scalar equations with a collocation setting that is not compiled into the D extension fall back to a Numba JIT solver. Every setting with divs ≤ 4 is compiled, so this row uses coll_setting=(5, [0, 3, 5]) — a 3-node rule comparable to the default — whose mesh intervals are 25 fine steps wide instead of 4. The fallback therefore takes ~6× fewer (larger) steps at equal \(N\) than the D rows above, and is still one to two orders of magnitude slower: its history sum is quadratic in the number of mesh intervals, while the D extension uses a blocked-FFT scheme. The one-time JIT compilation cost (seconds, on first call in a fresh environment) is excluded from the timings via a warmup round.

docs.title: Callable inputs
docs.text:
With callable inputs (mesh=) the solvers integrate the kernel numerically (Python + adaptive quadrature), so they are benchmarked on much smaller problems, sized by the number of mesh intervals \(M\) (each carrying len(coll_nodes) collocation nodes). The smooth rows use uniform meshes, on which the weights are assembled from one row (Toeplitz structure).

The two weakly singular rows solve the same Abel problem, \(K(u) = u^{-1/2}\) on a graded mesh, and show what the problem setup costs:

  • VIE-2 (weakly singular) is the slowest supported path: a kernel that only accepts scalars (1.0 / np.sqrt(u) if u > 0 else 0.0) and the singularity declared by location only (kernel_singularity=0.0). Every block the singularity touches is then integrated by adaptive quadrature, one scalar kernel call at a time, which is most of the cost.
  • VIE-2 (weakly singular, exponent declared) is the setup the docs recommend: a vectorised kernel (u**-0.5) and the exponent declared (kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5}), so those blocks use Gauss–Jacobi rules. It is 9–16× faster, more so as M grows, with the same accuracy.
Solver \ M 25 50 100 200 VIE-1 0.90 1.18 1.71 3.21 VIE-2 0.91 1.23 1.87 3.61 VIE-2 (vector, d=3) 1.10 1.52 2.47 6.54 VIDE 1.42 2.03 3.21 6.54 VIE-2 (weakly singular) 131 307 788 2291 VIE-2 (weakly singular, exponent declared) 13.5 28.4 61.6 131

docs.title: Two ways to give the inputs
docs.text:
Each solver accepts the kernel and the other input functions in one of two forms, chosen by their types (see Conventions for the full rules):

  • Arrays of samples at t = 0, dt, 2·dt, …, with the spacing given as dt. The kernel array holds K(u) at the lags u = 0, dt, …; the convolution lag is u = t − s. The solver builds a uniform mesh from the samples. The collocation nodes sit on samples and are chosen with coll_setting=(divs, choices), meaning nodes at choices / divs within each interval. By default the integrals use product quadrature, which works for every setting; see Product integration.
  • Callables kernel(u), g(t), a(t), with the mesh breakpoints given as mesh= (a 1-D array from 0 to T). Resolution is set by the mesh, which need not be uniform; the nodes are floats, coll_nodes=.

Every solver returns a VolterraSolution: sol.t and sol.y are the solution on the input grid (the sample times, or the mesh breakpoints), and sol(t) evaluates it anywhere in [0, T].

docs.title: solve_vie1
docs.text:
Solves \(g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) for unknown \(y(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.01
t = np.arange(0, 3.005, dt)            # 301 samples
g = np.sin(t)                          # g(0) must be 0 for a first-kind equation

sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.exp(t), g=g, dt=dt, coll_setting=(3, [1, 2, 3]))
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - (np.cos(t) - np.sin(t)))):.1e}")

The default nodes for VIE-1 are (3, [1, 2, 3]), so coll_setting could be left out here. Node sets for which the first-kind method diverges are rejected. The default mesh is 3² = 9 samples wide, wider than for the other two equations, because a first-kind equation amplifies noise in g by about the inverse of the mesh width; see Conventions.

docs.title: solve_vie2
docs.text:
Solves \(y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) for unknown \(y(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(0, 4.55, dt)             # 91 samples
g = np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=g, dt=dt, coll_setting=3)
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))):.1e}")

coll_setting=3 is short for (3, [0, 1, 2, 3]): every point the method admits.

docs.title: solve_vide
docs.text:
Solves \(y'(t) = a(t)y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\) for unknown \(y(t)\).

import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.01
t = np.arange(0, 0.91, dt)             # 91 samples
a = 1.0 / (1.0 + t**2)
g = (np.cos(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))
     - np.sin(t) / (1.0 + t**2))

sol = voles.solve_vide(kernel=np.exp(-t), a=a, g=g, y0=0.0, dt=dt)
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol.y - np.sin(t))):.1e}")

docs.title: Using the solution
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import voles

dt = 0.05
t = np.arange(0, 4.55, dt)
g = np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t))
sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=np.exp(-t), g=g, dt=dt)

sol(0.42)                              # a float: anywhere in [0, T]
sol(np.linspace(0, 4.5, 200))          # an array
sol(5.0)                               # nan: outside [0, T]
sol.to_ppoly().derivative()(0.42)      # y'(0.42), through scipy's PPoly
print(sol)

See Working with the solution for the collocation data, the coefficients and the values at breakpoints.

docs.title: Callable inputs
docs.text:
The same problem with callables, on a mesh you choose:

import numpy as np
import voles

sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u),
                       g=lambda t: np.sin(t) - 0.5 * (np.exp(-t) + np.sin(t) - np.cos(t)),
                       mesh=np.linspace(0, 4.5, 91))
print(sol(0.37), np.sin(0.37))

For a weakly singular kernel \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\) (e.g. Abel-type), declare the singularity and use optimal_graded_mesh to recover the full collocation convergence order. With the exponent known, the dict form kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5} switches the singular blocks from adaptive quadrature to deterministic Gauss–Jacobi rules, with an automatic fallback if the declared exponent turns out to be wrong. That is typically 3–10× faster than declaring only the location (kernel_singularity=0.0); a kernel that accepts arrays, like the one below, helps further (9–16× faster together, see Benchmarks):

import numpy as np
import voles

kernel = lambda u: u**-0.5
g = lambda t: np.sqrt(t) - 0.5 * np.pi * t        # exact y(t) = sqrt(t)

nodes = voles.radau_iia_nodes(3)
mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=30, order=len(nodes))
sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=nodes,
                       kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
tt = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
print(f"max error {np.max(np.abs(sol(tt) - np.sqrt(tt))):.1e}")

See Callable inputs and arbitrary meshes for more, including vector- and matrix-valued problems.

docs.title: Collocation node helpers
docs.text: Node sets for the coll_nodes parameter (callable inputs). Positions are floats in [0, 1]; these helpers build the classical families. For sampled inputs the nodes must sit on samples and are given as integers through coll_setting; see Conventions.

docs.title: gauss_legendre_nodes
docs.text:
gauss_legendre_nodes(p)

Return the p Gauss-Legendre collocation nodes on \([0, 1]\).

These interior nodes (none at 0 or 1) give the maximal collocation order. For a VIDE the solution superconverges to order \(2p\) at the mesh points. For VIE-2 the collocation solution itself does not: at an interior breakpoint the mean of its one-sided limits (the default of VolterraSolution) gains one order for \(p = 3\) (see the Conventions page, "Values at breakpoints"). For VIE-1 (first kind) Gauss nodes, being symmetric about \(1/2\), have amplification factor \(\rho_p = (-1)^p\): odd \(p\) keeps the full order \(p\), even \(p\) costs one order (see voles.solve_vie1, Notes). radau_iia_nodes have the full order for every \(p\).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p int

Number of nodes (the order of the collocation method), p >= 1.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (p,)

Node positions in \((0, 1)\), sorted ascending.

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.gauss_legendre_nodes(2)
array([0.21132487, 0.78867513])
Source code in src/voles/_functional.py 
def gauss_legendre_nodes(p: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return the ``p`` Gauss-Legendre collocation nodes on $[0, 1]$.

    These interior nodes (none at 0 or 1) give the maximal collocation order.
    For a **VIDE** the solution superconverges to order $2p$ at the mesh
    points. For **VIE-2** the collocation solution itself does not: at an
    interior breakpoint the mean of its one-sided limits (the default of
    `VolterraSolution`) gains one order for $p = 3$ (see the Conventions
    page, "Values at breakpoints"). For **VIE-1** (first kind) Gauss nodes,
    being symmetric about $1/2$, have amplification factor
    $\rho_p = (-1)^p$: odd $p$ keeps the full order $p$, even $p$ costs one
    order (see `voles.solve_vie1`, Notes). ``radau_iia_nodes`` have the full
    order for every $p$.

    Parameters
    ----------
    p : int
        Number of nodes (the order of the collocation method), ``p >= 1``.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (p,)
        Node positions in $(0, 1)$, sorted ascending.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.gauss_legendre_nodes(2)
    array([0.21132487, 0.78867513])
    """
    p = _check_node_count(p, minimum=1, name="Gauss-Legendre")
    x, _ = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(p)
    return np.sort(0.5 * (x + 1.0))

docs.title: radau_iia_nodes
docs.text:
radau_iia_nodes(p)

Return the p Radau IIA collocation nodes on \([0, 1]\).

The Radau IIA nodes include the right endpoint (1.0) and exclude 0. They give mesh-point superconvergence of order \(2p - 1\): for a VIDE directly, and for VIE-2 in the left limit at each breakpoint, which is the collocation value at the last node (sol(t, at_breakpoints="left"); the default mean has order \(p\)). The right-endpoint node also makes them a common choice for stiff VIDEs. For the default (discontinuous) VIE-1 method they are the recommended family: the endpoint node makes the amplification factor \(\rho_p = 0\), giving the full order \(p\) for every \(p\) (Gauss-Legendre nodes have \(\rho_p = (-1)^p\) and lose an order for even \(p\)). They do not suit continuous=True, where \(|\rho_{p-1}| = p\) and the method diverges for \(p \ge 2\) (see voles.solve_vie1, Notes).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p int

Number of nodes, p >= 1.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (p,)

Node positions in \((0, 1]\) (the last is exactly 1.0), sorted ascending.

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.radau_iia_nodes(2)
array([0.33333333, 1.        ])
Source code in src/voles/_functional.py 
def radau_iia_nodes(p: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return the ``p`` Radau IIA collocation nodes on $[0, 1]$.

    The Radau IIA nodes include the right endpoint (``1.0``) and exclude 0.
    They give mesh-point superconvergence of order $2p - 1$: for a **VIDE**
    directly, and for **VIE-2** in the left limit at each breakpoint, which
    is the collocation value at the last node
    (``sol(t, at_breakpoints="left")``; the default mean has order $p$). The
    right-endpoint node also makes them a common choice for stiff VIDEs. For
    the default (discontinuous) **VIE-1** method they are the recommended
    family: the endpoint node makes the amplification factor $\rho_p = 0$,
    giving the full order $p$ for every $p$ (Gauss-Legendre nodes have
    $\rho_p = (-1)^p$ and lose an order for even $p$). They do not suit
    ``continuous=True``, where $|\rho_{p-1}| = p$ and the method diverges for
    $p \ge 2$ (see `voles.solve_vie1`, Notes).

    Parameters
    ----------
    p : int
        Number of nodes, ``p >= 1``.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (p,)
        Node positions in $(0, 1]$ (the last is exactly ``1.0``), sorted
        ascending.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.radau_iia_nodes(2)
    array([0.33333333, 1.        ])
    """
    p = _check_node_count(p, minimum=1, name="Radau IIA")
    # On [-1, 1] the Radau IIA nodes are the roots of P_{p-1}(x) - P_p(x); one
    # of those roots is +1. Map the roots to [0, 1].
    c = np.zeros(p + 1)
    c[p - 1] += 1.0
    c[p] -= 1.0
    # legroots may return a complex-dtype array (tiny imaginary parts from the
    # companion-matrix eigensolver) on some numpy/LAPACK versions; these nodes
    # are mathematically real, so take the real part.
    x = np.polynomial.legendre.legroots(c).real
    nodes = np.sort(0.5 * (x + 1.0))
    nodes[-1] = 1.0  # pin the endpoint exactly
    return nodes

docs.title: lobatto_nodes
docs.text:
lobatto_nodes(p)

Return the p Gauss-Lobatto collocation nodes on \([0, 1]\) (p >= 2).

The Lobatto nodes include both endpoints (0.0 and 1.0) and have local order \(2p - 2\). Because 0 is included they suit VIE-2 and VIDE but not VIE-1, which forbids a node at \(t = 0\).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p int

Number of nodes, p >= 2.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (p,)

Node positions in \([0, 1]\) (the first is 0.0 and the last 1.0), sorted ascending.

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.lobatto_nodes(3)
array([0. , 0.5, 1. ])
Source code in src/voles/_functional.py 
def lobatto_nodes(p: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return the ``p`` Gauss-Lobatto collocation nodes on $[0, 1]$ (``p >= 2``).

    The Lobatto nodes include both endpoints (``0.0`` and ``1.0``) and have
    local order $2p - 2$. Because 0 is included they suit VIE-2 and VIDE but
    **not** VIE-1, which forbids a node at $t = 0$.

    Parameters
    ----------
    p : int
        Number of nodes, ``p >= 2``.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (p,)
        Node positions in $[0, 1]$ (the first is ``0.0`` and the last ``1.0``),
        sorted ascending.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.lobatto_nodes(3)
    array([0. , 0.5, 1. ])
    """
    p = _check_node_count(p, minimum=2, name="Lobatto")
    if p == 2:
        interior = np.array([])
    else:
        # The interior Lobatto nodes are the roots of P'_{p-1}.
        c = np.zeros(p)
        c[p - 1] = 1.0
        # .real: legroots may return complex dtype (see radau_iia_nodes); these
        # interior nodes are mathematically real.
        interior = np.polynomial.legendre.legroots(
            np.polynomial.legendre.legder(c)).real
    x = np.concatenate(([-1.0], interior, [1.0]))
    nodes = np.sort(0.5 * (x + 1.0))
    nodes[0] = 0.0   # pin the endpoints exactly
    nodes[-1] = 1.0
    return nodes

docs.title: Compiled collocation settings
docs.text: With the default quadrature="product" the solvers accept every valid coll_setting. With quadrature="collocation" they run routines compiled into the extension for a fixed list of settings (divs ≤ 4 in current builds); any other setting runs on the optional numba fallback (scalar problems only, with a PerformanceWarning) or raises NotImplementedError.

docs.title: optimal_graded_mesh
docs.text:
optimal_graded_mesh(*, alpha, t_end, n_intervals, order)

Return a graded mesh of n_intervals + 1 breakpoints suitable for a weakly singular convolution kernel \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in [0, 1)\).

Grading: \(t_n = T (n/M)^r\) with \(T\) = t_end, \(M\) = n_intervals and \(r = p / (1 - \alpha)\), where \(p\) = order is the order of the collocation method (the number of collocation nodes per interval). This recovers the optimal convergence order for Abel-type kernels (Brunner 2004, ch. 6). At alpha == 0 the kernel is non-singular and the solution smooth, so a uniform mesh (\(r = 1\)) is returned instead.

Pair the mesh with kernel_singularity={0.0: alpha} in the solver. Declaring the exponent, not only the location, lets the singular blocks use Gauss–Jacobi rules instead of adaptive quadrature, which is typically 3–10× faster.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default alpha float

Singularity exponent, in \([0, 1)\).

required t_end float

Right endpoint of the mesh (positive).

required n_intervals int

Number of intervals (positive). The returned array has length n_intervals + 1.

required order int

Order of the collocation method (positive). For a matched mesh, pass the number of collocation nodes the solver uses.

required

Returns:

Type Description ndarray of shape (n_intervals + 1,)

Strictly increasing breakpoints with [0] == 0 and [-1] == t_end.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If alpha is outside \([0, 1)\), t_end is not positive and finite, or n_intervals / order is less than 1.

TypeError

If alpha or t_end is not a real number, n_intervals / order is not an integer, or an argument is missing.

Examples:

>>> import voles
>>> voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=4, order=2)
array([0.        , 0.00390625, 0.0625    , 0.31640625, 1.        ])

Grade for the same order as the solver's collocation method. The solution of \(y(t) = 1 + \int_0^t (t-s)^{-1/2} y(s)\,ds\) is \(\operatorname{erfcx}(-\sqrt{\pi t})\):

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from scipy.special import erfcx
>>> nodes = voles.radau_iia_nodes(3)
>>> mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=60,
...                                  order=len(nodes))
>>> sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: u**-0.5, g=lambda t: np.ones_like(t),
...                        mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=nodes, kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
>>> print(f"relative error {abs(sol(1.0) / erfcx(-np.sqrt(np.pi)) - 1):.1e}")
relative error 1.3e-05
Source code in src/voles/_functional.py 
def optimal_graded_mesh(*, alpha: float, t_end: float, n_intervals: int,
                        order: int) -> np.ndarray:
    r"""Return a graded mesh of ``n_intervals + 1`` breakpoints suitable for a
    weakly singular convolution kernel $K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}$,
    $\alpha \in [0, 1)$.

    Grading: $t_n = T (n/M)^r$ with $T$ = ``t_end``, $M$ = ``n_intervals``
    and $r = p / (1 - \alpha)$, where $p$ = ``order`` is the order of the
    collocation method (the number of collocation nodes per interval). This
    recovers the optimal convergence order for Abel-type kernels (Brunner
    2004, ch. 6). At ``alpha == 0`` the kernel is non-singular and the
    solution smooth, so a uniform mesh ($r = 1$) is returned instead.

    Pair the mesh with ``kernel_singularity={0.0: alpha}`` in the solver.
    Declaring the exponent, not only the location, lets the singular blocks
    use Gauss–Jacobi rules instead of adaptive quadrature, which is
    typically 3–10× faster.

    Parameters
    ----------
    alpha : float
        Singularity exponent, in $[0, 1)$.
    t_end : float
        Right endpoint of the mesh (positive).
    n_intervals : int
        Number of intervals (positive). The returned array has length
        ``n_intervals + 1``.
    order : int
        Order of the collocation method (positive). For a matched mesh,
        pass the number of collocation nodes the solver uses.
    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of shape (n_intervals + 1,)
        Strictly increasing breakpoints with ``[0] == 0`` and
        ``[-1] == t_end``.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``alpha`` is outside $[0, 1)$, ``t_end`` is not positive and
        finite, or ``n_intervals`` / ``order`` is less than 1.
    TypeError
        If ``alpha`` or ``t_end`` is not a real number, ``n_intervals`` /
        ``order`` is not an integer, or an argument is missing.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import voles
    >>> voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=4, order=2)
    array([0.        , 0.00390625, 0.0625    , 0.31640625, 1.        ])

    Grade for the same order as the solver's collocation method. The
    solution of $y(t) = 1 + \int_0^t (t-s)^{-1/2} y(s)\,ds$ is
    $\operatorname{erfcx}(-\sqrt{\pi t})$:

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from scipy.special import erfcx
    >>> nodes = voles.radau_iia_nodes(3)
    >>> mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=60,
    ...                                  order=len(nodes))
    >>> sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=lambda u: u**-0.5, g=lambda t: np.ones_like(t),
    ...                        mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=nodes, kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
    >>> print(f"relative error {abs(sol(1.0) / erfcx(-np.sqrt(np.pi)) - 1):.1e}")
    relative error 1.3e-05
    """
    alpha = _v.real("alpha", alpha)
    if not 0.0 <= alpha < 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"alpha must satisfy 0 <= alpha < 1, got {alpha}")
    t_end = _v.real("t_end", t_end, positive=True,
                    value_msg=f"t_end must be positive and finite, got {t_end}")
    n_intervals = _v.integer("n_intervals", n_intervals, minimum=1,
                             value_msg=f"n_intervals must be a positive integer, got {n_intervals}")
    order = _v.integer("order", order, minimum=1,
                       type_msg=f"order must be a positive integer, got {order!r}",
                       value_msg=f"order must be a positive integer, got {order}")
    p = order
    # At alpha=0 the kernel is non-singular and the solution is smooth, so a
    # uniform mesh (r=1) is optimal; grading would only waste resolution near 0.
    r = p / (1.0 - alpha) if alpha > 0.0 else 1.0
    n = np.arange(n_intervals + 1, dtype=np.float64)
    return t_end * (n / n_intervals) ** r

class VolterraSolution:

    A piecewise polynomial on ``mesh`` (continuous or discontinuous at the
    breakpoints), together with its values on the grid the problem was posed
    on, the collocation data, and a record of the method. Call it to evaluate
    the solution anywhere in ``[0, T]``.

    Users don't construct it; every solver returns one.

    Attributes
    ----------
    t : ndarray, shape (K,)
        The grid the problem was posed on: the sample times ``n * dt`` for
        sampled inputs, the mesh breakpoints for callable inputs. Read-only.
    y : ndarray, shape (K, *shape)
        The solution at ``t``. At an interior breakpoint of a discontinuous
        solution this is the mean of the two one-sided limits, the same
        value ``sol(t)`` gives. Writable; changing it doesn't change the
        solution.
    mesh : ndarray, shape (M + 1,)
        The breakpoints ``0 = t_0 < ... < t_M = T``.
    node_times : ndarray, shape (M, p)
        The collocation times actually used. For sampled inputs the final
        interval may be longer than the others, and its nodes sit on its
        own sample grid, so they can differ from ``mesh[n] + nodes * h_n``.
    node_values : ndarray, shape (M, p, *shape)
        The solution at ``node_times``: the collocation values.
    coefficients : ndarray, shape (M, P, *shape)
        Interval n's polynomial in the local variable
        ``x = (t - mesh[n]) / (mesh[n+1] - mesh[n])`` in ``[0, 1]``, as
        monomial coefficients, lowest degree first.
    nodes : ndarray, shape (p,)
        The nominal node positions in ``[0, 1]``, sorted.
    coll_setting : tuple or None
        ``(divs, choices)`` for sampled inputs, ``None`` for callable inputs.
    dt, samples_per_interval, quadrature : float, int, str or None
        For sampled inputs: the sample spacing, the mesh width in samples, and
        ``"product"`` or ``"collocation"``. ``None`` for callable inputs.
    equation : {"vie1", "vie2", "vide"}
    regime : {"sampled", "functional"}
    continuous : bool
        Whether the solution space is continuous across breakpoints (VIDE,
        and VIE-1 with ``continuous=True``).

    Here ``shape`` is ``()`` for scalar problems, ``(d,)`` for vector
    problems and ``(d, m)`` for m right-hand sides. The dtype is complex for
    complex problems.

    See Also
    --------
    - [solve_vie1][voles.solve_vie1], [solve_vie2][voles.solve_vie2],
      [solve_vide][voles.solve_vide]: the solvers that return it.
    - [to_ppoly][voles.VolterraSolution.to_ppoly]: derivatives, integrals and roots.

    Examples
    --------
    $g(t) = \int_0^t e^{-(t-s)} y(s)\,ds$ with $g = \sin t$ has the solution
    $y = \cos t + \sin t$. Solve it on four intervals:

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> import voles
    >>> sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=lambda u: np.exp(-u), g=np.sin,
    ...                        mesh=np.linspace(0, 1, 5))
    >>> sol.mesh
    array([0.  , 0.25, 0.5 , 0.75, 1.  ])
    >>> sol.coefficients.shape, sol.node_times.shape
    ((4, 3), (4, 3))

    Evaluate anywhere in $[0, T]$; outside it the result is NaN:

    >>> print(f"{sol(0.3):.5f}  {np.cos(0.3) + np.sin(0.3):.5f}")
    1.25088  1.25086
    >>> sol(1.5)
    nan

    This (discontinuous) solution has two one-sided limits at each interior
    breakpoint; ``sol(t)`` gives their mean unless asked otherwise:

    >>> for side in ("left", "mean", "right"):
    ...     print(side, f"{sol(0.5, at_breakpoints=side):.5f}")
    left 1.35708
    mean 1.35703
    right 1.35697

    Integrals and derivatives through `scipy.interpolate.PPoly`:

    >>> print(f"{sol.to_ppoly().integrate(0, 1):.6f}  {np.sin(1) - np.cos(1) + 1:.6f}")
    1.301168  1.301169
    """

    equation: Literal["vie1", "vie2", "vide"]
    regime: Literal["sampled", "functional"]
    continuous: bool
    coll_setting: Optional[Tuple[int, List[int]]]
    # State set by `_build` (and restored by unpickling).
    _coef: np.ndarray
    _mesh: np.ndarray
    _nodes: np.ndarray
    _local_nodes: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _node_times: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _node_values: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _node_layout: Optional[tuple]
    _y: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _t: Optional[np.ndarray]
    _dt: Optional[float]
    _n: Optional[int]
    _Q: Optional[int]
    _quadrature: Optional[str]
    _d: int
    _m: int

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        raise TypeError("VolterraSolution objects are returned by the solvers; "
                        "they are not constructed directly")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ building

    @classmethod
    def _build(cls, *, coefficients, mesh, nodes, equation, regime, continuous, d, m,
               local_nodes=None, node_times=None, node_layout=None, coll_setting=None,
               y=None, node_values=None, dt=None, n_samples=None, copy_mesh=True,
               samples_per_interval=None, quadrature=None):
        """The solvers' constructor.

        ``local_nodes`` (M, p): each interval's node positions in its local
        variable, which `node_values` evaluates at when the solver hasn't
        supplied them; ``node_times`` (M, p) the times. Instead of both, the
        sampled builder passes ``node_layout`` (a tuple for `_sampled_layout`),
        and they are computed on first access. Sampled regime: ``y`` (the
        values on the sample grid), ``dt`` and ``n_samples`` are required.
        Functional regime: ``y`` is computed on first access, at the
        breakpoints. ``copy_mesh=False`` is for a mesh voles built itself."""
        if equation not in _EQUATIONS or regime not in _REGIMES:
            raise ValueError(f"bad equation/regime {equation!r}/{regime!r}")
        self = cls.__new__(cls)
        coef = np.asarray(coefficients)
        if not np.issubdtype(coef.dtype, np.complexfloating):
            coef = coef.astype(float, copy=False)
        self._coef = _read_only(coef, copy=False)          # computed by the engine
        self._mesh = _read_only(mesh, dtype=float, copy=copy_mesh)   # may alias user data
        M = len(self._mesh) - 1
        if self._coef.shape[0] != M or M < 1:
            raise ValueError(f"{self._coef.shape[0]} coefficient blocks for {M} mesh intervals")
        self._node_layout = node_layout
        if node_layout is None:
            self._set_node_arrays(local_nodes, node_times)
        else:
            self._local_nodes = self._node_times = None
        self._nodes = _read_only(np.sort(np.asarray(nodes, dtype=float)))
        self._node_values = (None if node_values is None
                             else _read_only(node_values, copy=False))   # engine output
        self.equation = equation
        self.regime = regime
        self.continuous = bool(continuous)
        self.coll_setting = (None if coll_setting is None
                             else (int(coll_setting[0]), [int(c) for c in coll_setting[1]]))
        self._d, self._m = int(d), int(m)
        if regime == "sampled":
            if y is None or dt is None or n_samples is None:
                raise ValueError("the sampled regime needs y, dt and n_samples")
            self._y = np.asarray(y)
            self._dt, self._n = float(dt), int(n_samples)
            self._Q = None if samples_per_interval is None else int(samples_per_interval)
            self._quadrature = quadrature
        else:
            self._y = None if y is None else np.asarray(y)
            self._dt = self._n = self._Q = self._quadrature = None
        self._t = None
        return self

    def __getstate__(self):
        state = self.__dict__.copy()
        state["_t"] = None               # rebuilt on demand
        return state

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ attributes

    @property
    def mesh(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._mesh

    @property
    def coefficients(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._coef

    def _set_node_arrays(self, local_nodes, node_times):
        self._local_nodes = _read_only(local_nodes, dtype=float, copy=False)
        self._node_times = _read_only(node_times, dtype=float, copy=False)
        if (self._local_nodes.shape != self._node_times.shape
                or self._node_times.shape[0] != len(self._mesh) - 1):
            raise ValueError("node arrays must have shape (M, p)")

    def _nodes_local_and_times(self) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
        if self._local_nodes is None or self._node_times is None:
            assert self._node_layout is not None
            self._set_node_arrays(*_sampled_layout(*self._node_layout))
        assert self._local_nodes is not None and self._node_times is not None
        return self._local_nodes, self._node_times

    @property
    def node_times(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._nodes_local_and_times()[1]

    @property
    def nodes(self) -> np.ndarray:
        return self._nodes

    # Sampled-regime settings (None for callable inputs). getattr: a 0.11.0
    # pickle has no _Q / _quadrature.
    @property
    def dt(self) -> Optional[float]:
        return self._dt

    @property
    def samples_per_interval(self) -> Optional[int]:
        return getattr(self, "_Q", None)

    @property
    def quadrature(self) -> Optional[str]:
        return getattr(self, "_quadrature", None)

    @property
    def t(self) -> np.ndarray:
        t = self._t
        if t is None:
            if self.regime == "sampled":
                assert self._n is not None and self._dt is not None
                t = _read_only(np.arange(self._n) * self._dt)
            else:
                t = self._mesh
            self._t = t
        return t

    @property
    def y(self) -> np.ndarray:
        y = self._y
        if y is None:                             # functional regime, first access
            y = np.asarray(self(self._mesh))
            self._y = y
        return y

    @property
    def node_values(self) -> np.ndarray:
        nv = self._node_values
        if nv is None:
            x = self._nodes_local_and_times()[0]                # (M, p)
            c = self._coef                                      # (M, P, *cs)
            extra = (1,) * (c.ndim - 2)
            xb = x.reshape(x.shape + extra)
            out = np.broadcast_to(c[:, -1][:, None], x.shape + c.shape[2:])
            for k in range(c.shape[1] - 2, -1, -1):
                out = out * xb + c[:, k][:, None]
            nv = self._node_values = _read_only(out)
        return nv

    @property
    def _shape(self):
        return self._coef.shape[2:]

    # ------------------------------------------------------------ evaluation

    def _horner(self, idx, x):
        """Interval ``idx[i]``'s polynomial at local ``x[i]``, without
        gathering an (n, P, *shape) copy of the coefficients."""
        c = self._coef
        xb = x.reshape(x.shape + (1,) * (c.ndim - 2))
        out = c[idx, -1]                  # a fresh gather, so updating in place is safe
        for k in range(c.shape[1] - 2, -1, -1):
            out *= xb                     # same operations as out = out * x + c_k
            out += c[idx, k]
        return out

    def __call__(self, t: ArrayLike, *,
                 at_breakpoints: Literal["mean", "left", "right"] = "mean"
                 ) -> Union[float, complex, np.ndarray]:
        """Evaluate the solution at ``t`` (scalar or array).

        Parameters
        ----------
        t : float or array_like
            Times in ``[0, T]``. Points outside (beyond a rounding-level
            tolerance) give NaN; the solution is never extrapolated.
        at_breakpoints : {"mean", "left", "right"}, optional
            The value at an interior breakpoint, where a discontinuous
            solution has two one-sided limits: their mean (default), the
            limit from the left, or from the right. A point within a few
            ulps of a breakpoint counts as that breakpoint. For a continuous
            solution the three agree to rounding.

        Returns
        -------
        float, complex or ndarray
            A scalar ``t`` gives a Python float or complex for scalar problems
            and an array of shape ``shape`` otherwise; an array ``t`` gives an
            array of shape ``t.shape + shape``.
        """
        mode = _v.choice("at_breakpoints", at_breakpoints, _AT_BREAKPOINTS)
        scalar_input = np.ndim(t) == 0
        t_arr = np.asarray(t, dtype=float)
        tf = t_arr.ravel()
        bps = self._mesh
        M = len(bps) - 1
        idx = np.clip(np.searchsorted(bps, tf, side="right") - 1, 0, M - 1)
        x = (tf - bps[idx]) / (bps[idx + 1] - bps[idx])
        out = self._horner(idx, x)
        if M > 1 and tf.size:
            interior = bps[1:-1]
            tol = 4.0 * np.spacing(np.abs(interior))
            j = np.searchsorted(interior, tf)
            lo, hi = np.clip(j - 1, 0, M - 2), np.clip(j, 0, M - 2)
            hit_hi = np.abs(tf - interior[hi]) <= tol[hi]
            hit_lo = np.abs(tf - interior[lo]) <= tol[lo]
            at = hit_hi | hit_lo
            if at.any():
                k = np.where(hit_hi, hi, lo)[at] + 1          # interval to the right
                n = k.size
                left = self._horner(k - 1, np.ones(n))
                right = self._horner(k, np.zeros(n))
                out = np.array(out, copy=True)
                out[at] = (0.5 * (left + right) if mode == "mean"
                           else left if mode == "left" else right)
        # Defined on [t_0, t_M] only. The tolerance is relative to the solved
        # interval, but never below a few ulps of the endpoints, so an exactly
        # computed T passes.
        tol_end = max(1e-12 * float(bps[-1] - bps[0]),
                      4.0 * float(np.spacing(np.max(np.abs(bps)))))
        outside = (tf < bps[0] - tol_end) | (tf > bps[-1] + tol_end)
        if outside.any():
            out = np.array(out, copy=True)
            out[outside] = np.nan
        if scalar_input:
            v = out[0]
            return v.item() if not self._shape else v
        return out.reshape(t_arr.shape + self._shape)

    def to_ppoly(self) -> PPoly:
        """The solution as a `scipy.interpolate.PPoly`.

        Useful for derivatives (``.derivative()``), antiderivatives and
        integrals (``.antiderivative()``, ``.integrate(a, b)``) and roots.
        The trailing axes are the problem's ``shape``. PPoly is
        right-continuous at breakpoints (it uses the right-hand interval's
        polynomial there), and returns NaN outside ``[0, T]``.
        """
        from scipy.interpolate import PPoly
        c = self._coef
        h = np.diff(self._mesh)
        P = c.shape[1]
        scale = h[:, None] ** -np.arange(P)[None, :]             # (M, P): 1 / h^k
        scaled = c * scale.reshape(scale.shape + (1,) * (c.ndim - 2))
        pc = np.ascontiguousarray(np.moveaxis(scaled, 1, 0)[::-1])   # (P, M, *shape)
        # Copies: scipy's Cython routines (antiderivative, roots) need writable
        # buffers, and the solution's arrays are read-only.
        return PPoly(pc, np.array(self._mesh), extrapolate=False)

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        M = len(self._mesh) - 1
        nodes = (f"coll_setting={self.coll_setting}" if self.coll_setting is not None
                 else "coll_nodes=[" + ", ".join(f"{c:.4g}" for c in self._nodes) + "]")
        if self.samples_per_interval is not None:
            nodes += f", samples_per_interval={self.samples_per_interval}, {self.quadrature}"
        shape = f", shape={self._shape}" if self._shape else ""
        return (f"<VolterraSolution {self.equation}, {self.regime}, {M} intervals on "
                f"[0, {self._mesh[-1]:.6g}], degree {self._coef.shape[1] - 1}, {nodes}"
                f"{shape}, {self._coef.dtype}>")

    idx = np.clip(np.searchsorted(bps, tf, side="right") - 1, 0, M - 1)
    x = (tf - bps[idx]) / (bps[idx + 1] - bps[idx])
    out = self._horner(idx, x)
    if M > 1 and tf.size:
        interior = bps[1:-1]
        tol = 4.0 * np.spacing(np.abs(interior))
        j = np.searchsorted(interior, tf)
        lo, hi = np.clip(j - 1, 0, M - 2), np.clip(j, 0, M - 2)
        hit_hi = np.abs(tf - interior[hi]) <= tol[hi]
        hit_lo = np.abs(tf - interior[lo]) <= tol[lo]
        at = hit_hi | hit_lo
        if at.any():
            k = np.where(hit_hi, hi, lo)[at] + 1          # interval to the right
            n = k.size
            left = self._horner(k - 1, np.ones(n))
            right = self._horner(k, np.zeros(n))
            out = np.array(out, copy=True)
            out[at] = (0.5 * (left + right) if mode == "mean"
                       else left if mode == "left" else right)
    # Defined on [t_0, t_M] only. The tolerance is relative to the solved
    # interval, but never below a few ulps of the endpoints, so an exactly
    # computed T passes.
    tol_end = max(1e-12 * float(bps[-1] - bps[0]),
                  4.0 * float(np.spacing(np.max(np.abs(bps)))))
    outside = (tf < bps[0] - tol_end) | (tf > bps[-1] + tol_end)
    if outside.any():
        out = np.array(out, copy=True)
        out[outside] = np.nan
    if scalar_input:
        v = out[0]
        return v.item() if not self._shape else v
    return out.reshape(t_arr.shape + self._shape)

def to_ppoly(self) -> PPoly:
    """The solution as a `scipy.interpolate.PPoly`.

    Useful for derivatives (``.derivative()``), antiderivatives and
    integrals (``.antiderivative()``, ``.integrate(a, b)``) and roots.
    The trailing axes are the problem's ``shape``. PPoly is
    right-continuous at breakpoints (it uses the right-hand interval's
    polynomial there), and returns NaN outside ``[0, T]``.
    """
    from scipy.interpolate import PPoly
    c = self._coef
    h = np.diff(self._mesh)
    P = c.shape[1]
    scale = h[:, None] ** -np.arange(P)[None, :]             # (M, P): 1 / h^k
    scaled = c * scale.reshape(scale.shape + (1,) * (c.ndim - 2))
    pc = np.ascontiguousarray(np.moveaxis(scaled, 1, 0)[::-1])   # (P, M, *shape)
    # Copies: scipy's Cython routines (antiderivative, roots) need writable
    # buffers, and the solution's arrays are read-only.
    return PPoly(pc, np.array(self._mesh), extrapolate=False)

The discontinuous method converges iff its amplification factor \(\rho_m = (-1)^m \prod_{i=1}^{m} (1 - c_i)/c_i\) satisfies \(|\rho_m| \le 1\), and the continuous one iff \(\rho_{m-1} = (-1)^m \prod_{i<m} (1 - c_i)/c_i\) does, with \(c_m = 1\) (Brunner 2004, Theorems 2.4.2 and 2.4.5). ...                        mesh=mesh, kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
>>> print(f"{sol(0.25):.4f}")

        ``(d,)`` or ``(d, m)``. Default zero.
    continuous : bool, optional
        Use the continuous collocation method (Brunner's $S_m^{(0)}$, degree
        $m$ on $m$ nodes, one order higher) instead of the default
        discontinuous one ($S_{m-1}^{(-1)}$). Needs ``y0`` and a node at the
        right end of each interval.
    y0 : array_like, optional
        $y(0)$, for ``continuous=True`` only. Scalar, ``(d,)`` or ``(d, m)``.
    dt : float, optional
        Sampled inputs: the sample spacing. Default 1.0.
    coll_setting : int or (int, sequence of int), optional
        Sampled inputs: the collocation nodes ``choices / divs`` as
        ``(divs, choices)``, with choices in ``1..divs``, or a bare ``divs``
        meaning every point ``1..divs``. ``divs`` also sets the mesh
        width (see ``samples_per_interval``). Default ``(3, [1, 2, 3])``.
    quadrature : {"product", "collocation"}, optional
        Sampled inputs: how the integrals are evaluated from the samples.
        ``"product"`` (default) integrates a piecewise polynomial
        interpolant of the kernel exactly and accepts any mesh width and
        node set. ``"collocation"`` applies the interpolatory rule on the
        nodes; it is faster but fixes the mesh at ``divs**2`` samples, runs
        only compiled settings (or the numba fallback), and is unstable when
        $K(0)$ is small.
    samples_per_interval : int, optional
        Sampled inputs: samples per mesh interval. A multiple of ``divs``
        with product quadrature; default ``divs**2``, because a first-kind
        inversion amplifies data errors by about the inverse of the mesh
        width. Must be ``divs**2`` with collocation quadrature.
    kernel_interp_degree : int, optional
        Sampled inputs, product quadrature: the degree of the kernel
        interpolant. Default: the number of nodes.
    mesh : array_like, optional
        Callable inputs: the mesh breakpoints, strictly increasing from 0 to
        $T$. Required for callable inputs.
    coll_nodes : array_like, optional
        Callable inputs: node positions in $(0, 1]$, e.g.
        ``voles.radau_iia_nodes(3)``. Default ``[1/3, 2/3, 1]``.
    kernel_singularity : float, list, dict or callable, optional
        Callable inputs: where the kernel is weakly singular, in
        $u = t - s$: a location, a list of locations, ``{location: alpha}``
        for $K \sim |u - u_0|^{-\alpha}$, or a callable returning the
        singular $s$-locations for a time $t$. Declare the exponent when you
        know it: the blocks the singularity touches then use Gauss–Jacobi
        rules instead of adaptive quadrature, typically 3–10× faster for the
        whole solve.
    reuse_adaptive_blocks : bool, optional
        Callable inputs: on a uniform mesh, reuse adaptive-quadrature blocks
        across mesh intervals. Default True.

    Returns
    -------
    VolterraSolution
        The solution: ``sol.t`` and ``sol.y`` on the input grid (the samples,
        or the mesh breakpoints), ``sol(t)`` anywhere in $[0, T]$, plus the
        collocation data and coefficients.

    Raises
    ------
    TypeError
        An argument of the wrong type (a float where an integer is needed, a
        non-bool flag, a non-numeric array), or a required one missing.
    ValueError
        A wrong value: shapes that don't fit, an option from the other
        regime, a node set for which the method diverges, NaN or inf in
        the data, too few samples for one mesh interval.
    NotImplementedError
        Mixed callable and sampled inputs, or an uncompiled setting under
        ``quadrature="collocation"`` with no fallback.
    numpy.linalg.LinAlgError
        A collocation system is singular (e.g. an identically zero kernel).

    Warns
    -----
    AccuracyWarning
        $g(0) \ne 0$; a node set with $\rho = +1$ (one order lower);
        $K(0)$ too small for collocation quadrature; a singularity declared
        on a uniform mesh.
    PerformanceWarning
        The numba fallback is used; or a declared exponent in
        ``kernel_singularity`` failed its accuracy check, so the singular
        blocks used adaptive quadrature.
    VolesWarning
        A ``kernel_singularity`` location outside $[0, T]$.

    See Also
    --------
    - [solve_vie2][voles.solve_vie2], [solve_vide][voles.solve_vide]: the other two
      equations.
    - [VolterraSolution][voles.VolterraSolution]: the returned object.
    - [optimal_graded_mesh][voles.optimal_graded_mesh]: a mesh for a weakly singular
      kernel.
    - [radau_iia_nodes][voles.radau_iia_nodes]: node sets for ``coll_nodes``.

    Notes
    -----
    The regime is chosen by the input types: arrays give the sampled regime
    (``dt``, ``coll_setting``, ``quadrature``, ``samples_per_interval``,
    ``kernel_interp_degree`` apply), callables the functional regime
    (``mesh``, ``coll_nodes``, ``kernel_singularity``,
    ``reuse_adaptive_blocks`` apply). An option from the other regime is
    an error. Mixing callable and sampled inputs is not supported yet.

    The discontinuous method converges iff its amplification factor
    $\rho_m = (-1)^m \prod_{i=1}^{m} (1 - c_i)/c_i$ satisfies
    $|\rho_m| \le 1$, and the continuous one iff
    $\rho_{m-1} = (-1)^m \prod_{i<m} (1 - c_i)/c_i$ does, with $c_m = 1$
    (Brunner 2004, Theorems 2.4.2 and 2.4.5). The order is full for
    $-1 \le \rho < 1$ and one lower at $\rho = +1$. Radau IIA nodes have
    $\rho_m = 0$; Gauss-Legendre nodes have $\rho_m = (-1)^m$.

    Examples
    --------
    Sampled data: with $K = 1$ and $g(t) = \sin t$ the solution is
    $y = \cos t$.

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> import voles
    >>> t = np.linspace(0, 2, 201)
    >>> sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.ones_like(t), g=np.sin(t), dt=t[1])
    >>> sol
    <VolterraSolution vie1, sampled, 22 intervals on [0, 2], degree 2, ...>
    >>> sol.y.shape
    (201,)
    >>> print(f"{sol(1.0):.6f}  {np.cos(1.0):.6f}")
    0.540303  0.540302

    Callables: Abel's equation, $K(u) = u^{-1/2}$ and $g(t) = \pi t / 2$,
    whose solution $y = \sqrt{t}$ has an unbounded derivative at 0. Declare
    the singularity and grade the mesh to match it:

    >>> mesh = voles.optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, t_end=1.0, n_intervals=16, order=3)
    >>> sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=lambda u: u**-0.5, g=lambda t: np.pi / 2 * t,
    ...                        mesh=mesh, kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5})
    >>> print(f"{sol(0.25):.4f}")
    0.5000
    """
    return _solve("vie1", kernel=kernel, g=g, y0=y0, continuous=continuous, dt=dt,
                  coll_setting=coll_setting, quadrature=quadrature,
                  samples_per_interval=samples_per_interval,
                  kernel_interp_degree=kernel_interp_degree, mesh=mesh, coll_nodes=coll_nodes,
                  kernel_singularity=kernel_singularity,
                  reuse_adaptive_blocks=reuse_adaptive_blocks)

Bases: UserWarning

Base class of every warning voles emits.

Each diagnostic is issued once per solver call with warnings.warn, attributed to the line that called the solver, so the standard warnings filters apply. Python shows a given warning once per calling line by default.

See Also
  • AccuracyWarning, PerformanceWarning: the two kinds.

Examples:

A first-kind equation with \(g(0) \ne 0\) has no bounded solution, so voles warns. Make that an error:

>>> import warnings
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import voles
>>> with warnings.catch_warnings():
...     warnings.simplefilter("error", voles.AccuracyWarning)
...     voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.ones(10), g=np.ones(10))
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
voles.AccuracyWarning: g(0) is not zero ...

or silence every voles diagnostic in a block:

>>> with warnings.catch_warnings():
...     warnings.simplefilter("ignore", voles.VolesWarning)
...     sol = voles.solve_vie1(kernel=np.ones(10), g=np.ones(10))

docs.title: 1. Goal and shape of the result
docs.text:
Three public solvers replace six:

```python notest sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=K, g=g, dt=0.01) # sampled inputs sol = voles.solve_vie2(kernel=k, g=f, mesh=bps) # callable inputs sol.t, sol.y # the grid the problem was posed on, and the values there sol(t) # dense output sol.node_times, sol.node_values, sol.coefficients, sol.to_ppoly()


Two release steps:

- **0.11.0**: the new API, warnings through `warnings`, every bug-level fix,
  and the six old functions kept as deprecation wrappers. Each wrapper
  translates its kwargs, calls the new API, and converts the result back to
  the old return type. Old code keeps running with **bitwise-identical
  results**, with one accepted exception (dense evaluation at exact interior
  breakpoints, D5). Each wrapper call raises a `DeprecationWarning` that
  names the new call.
- **1.0.0**: delete the wrappers and other deprecated names, ship `py.typed`,
  and put the stability policy into force.

This matches the process agreed on 2026-10-12: deprecate in 0.11, remove in
1.0, with a signature-snapshot test as the guard.

**No D changes.** The D ABI already takes what both cores need. All the work
is in Python.

### Two input regimes, one documented rule

The cores stay two different discretisations, and the API says so in one
place instead of in the function names:

| | **sampled** | **functional** |
|---|---|---|
| Selected when | any of `kernel`, `g`, `a` is an array | all given inputs are callables |
| Grid argument | `dt` (sample spacing, default 1.0); the solver builds the mesh | `mesh` (breakpoints starting at 0, required); the user owns the mesh |
| Nodes | `coll_setting=(divs, [choices])` or `coll_setting=divs`: integers on the sample grid | `coll_nodes=`: floats in [0,1] ((0,1] for VIE-1) |
| Options that apply only here | `coll_setting`, `quadrature`, `samples_per_interval`, `kernel_interp_degree` | `coll_nodes`, `kernel_singularity`, `reuse_adaptive_blocks` |
| `sol.t` | the sample times n·dt, n = 0…N−1 | the mesh breakpoints |
| Core (today's code) | `solvers.py` internals + D | `_callable_solvers.py` internals + D/scipy |

- **Crossed inputs:** an option belonging to the other regime raises a
  `ValueError` that says which regime was inferred and why. Example: "kernel
  is an array, so the problem is sampled; mesh= is for callable inputs, use
  dt= and coll_setting=".
- **`dt` with `mesh`:** a `dt` other than the default, passed with `mesh`,
  raises. An explicit `dt=1.0` can't be told apart from the default and is
  ignored; this is accepted.
- **Mixed inputs** (e.g. a callable K with sampled g) are rejected in 1.0
  with `NotImplementedError`, and the contract doc reserves them. Adding them
  later breaks nothing. When added, their nodes sit on the sample grid, so
  they take `coll_setting`.

---

## 2. Decisions (settled 2026-10-31)

**D1. PEP 8 identifiers everywhere.**
- Public: `solve_vie1`, `solve_vie2`, `solve_vide`; `optimal_graded_mesh`
  parameters `T` → `t_end` and `M` → `n_intervals` (`alpha` and `order`
  stay).
- Private *function* names are renamed too (e.g. `_build_W_scalar` →
  `_build_w_scalar`).
- Maths-notation locals (`N`, `M`, `Q`, `K`, `W`, `K_real`) stay; PEP 8's
  "foolish consistency" clause covers them.
- The new names also make the deprecation clean: the old names keep their
  old return types throughout 0.11.

**D2. `dt: float = 1.0`**, sampled regime only. `mesh` is required in the
functional regime.

**D3. Nodes, one argument per regime.**
- Sampled: `coll_setting=(divs, [choices])`, exactly today's
  `coll_divs`/`coll_choices`.
  - A bare `coll_setting=divs` means every point the method admits: 1..q
    for VIE-1, 0..q otherwise.
  - `None` gives the default: VIE-1 `(3, [1,2,3])`; VIE-2/VIDE
    `(2, [0,1,2])`.
  - Any length-2 sequence is accepted. Integers only (NumPy ints allowed);
    floats raise `TypeError`.
  - The choices-only form is gone, which removes one of F22's three
    inference rules.
  - Why integers: `divs` also fixes the mesh. It is `divs²` samples wide
    under collocation quadrature, and it sets the default and the allowed
    multiples of `samples_per_interval` under product quadrature. So float
    node positions would lose information, and nudging a float could
    silently select an unrelated method.
- Functional: `coll_nodes=` floats, as today. `coll_setting` is *not*
  accepted there (F8: the same name must not mean two things). The
  defaults are the same node positions.
- `samples_per_interval` (renamed from `mesh_samples`) keeps today's rules:
  any multiple of `divs` under product quadrature, exactly `divs²` under
  collocation quadrature, and today's defaults.
- Docstring caveat: a bare `divs` with VIE-1 `continuous=True` gives
  ρ = (−1)^q, so for even q the method is admitted at reduced order, with an
  `AccuracyWarning`. Same as today's `coll_divs` alone.

**D4. VIE-1 continuous method: `continuous: bool = False` plus `y0`.**
`y0` is required when `continuous=True` and a `ValueError` otherwise (today
it is a printed warning). The initial value is called `y0` in all three
solvers (F13).

**D5. Returned object: one merged class, `VolterraSolution`** (§3). There is
no separate result-plus-solution pair: we have no solver diagnostics, since
failures raise, so everything the result would hold describes the piecewise
polynomial.
- **Breakpoint convention:** at interior breakpoints, `sol.y` and `sol(t)`
  report the *mean* of the two one-sided limits by default.
  `sol(t, at_breakpoints="left"|"right")` gives either limit.
- *Final (decided 2026-11-01):* "mean" is the 1.0 default. Iterated solutions come
  after 1.0 as an additive keyword, so they don't reopen it.
- Measured error at interior breakpoints, K = e⁻ᵘ, y = cos t on [0,4]
  (scripts in that day's scratchpad, `breakpoint_sides*.py`):

  | Method | left | right | mean |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | VIE-1 default {1/3,2/3,1} | O(h³) | O(h³) | **O(h⁴)** |
  | VIE-1 Radau IIA p=3 | O(h³) | O(h³) | O(h³), best constant |
  | VIE-2 default {0,1/2,1} | O(h⁴) | identical (\|L−R\| ≈ 1e-16) | identical |
  | VIE-2 Gauss p=3 | O(h³) | O(h³) | **O(h⁴)** |
  | VIE-2 Radau IIA p=3 | **O(h⁵)** | O(h³) | O(h³) |

  Today the sampled grid output already averages (on both the D path and
  the product path), while `sol(t)` takes the right limit.
- **The 0.11 wrappers** take the new convention for dense evaluation at
  exact interior breakpoints. This was accepted as an accuracy improvement;
  on sampled VIE-1 data the error at breakpoints goes from 2.8e-7 to
  3.6e-9. *Superseded by the lighter engine (Phase 3/5):* the wrappers return
  the unchanged 0.10 object, so 0.10 dense evaluation doesn't change at all.
  `VolterraSolution`'s compatibility aliases were therefore dropped
  (`mesh_breakpoints`, `polynomials`, `len`, indexing, iteration). The class
  was never released, so no deprecation was needed.
- **`to_ppoly()` is added. `to_polynomials()` and the `Polynomial` list are
  removed.** The list survives in 0.11 only behind the deprecated
  `.polynomials`, indexing and iteration aliases.

**D6. `sol.t`/`sol.y` are the grid the problem was posed on.** That's the
sample times in the sampled regime and the mesh breakpoints in the
functional regime. The collocation data is `node_times`/`node_values` in
both regimes. The flattened `(M·p,)` node grid I first proposed is dropped:
with the default VIE-2/VIDE nodes it repeats every interior breakpoint,
which breaks `np.interp`/`searchsorted`.

**D7. Warnings:** `VolesWarning(UserWarning)` as the base, with
`AccuracyWarning` and `PerformanceWarning` under it.

| Site(s) | Category |
|---|---|
| ρ = 1 reduced order (`solvers.py:156`) | Accuracy |
| VIE-1 g(0) ≠ 0 (`:193`, `:197`) | Accuracy |
| VIE-1 K(0) small/singular, collocation quadrature (`:252`) | Accuracy |
| singularity declared on a uniform mesh (`_callable_solvers.py:2425`) | Accuracy |
| singularity location outside [0, T] (`:2417`) | base `VolesWarning` |
| Numba fallback (`solvers.py:744, 1387, 1650`) | Performance |
| stale D extension lacking the lag-block driver (`_product.py:605`) | Performance |
| `soln_init_value` ignored (5 sites) | becomes a `ValueError` (D4); a `VolesWarning` inside the wrappers until 1.0 |

**D8.** Mixed inputs are rejected in 1.0 and reserved (§1).

**D9.** Deprecations use `DeprecationWarning`.

**D10.** These names stay: `kernel_singularity`, `reuse_adaptive_blocks`,
`kernel_interp_degree`, `quadrature`. `mesh_samples` →
`samples_per_interval`. `optimal_graded_mesh(T=, M=)` is accepted with a
warning in 0.11.

**D11.** Every parameter stays keyword-only.

**D12. Non-finite inputs:**
- Arrays: raise `ValueError`.
- Callable `g` and `a`: checked at the collocation times.
- Kernel callables: not checked, and the docs say so. A singular kernel
  legitimately returns inf at u = 0, and the quadrature never samples there.

**Open: iterated solution.** For VIE-2, the iterated solution is
u_it(t) = g(t) + ∫₀ᵗ K(t−s) u_h(s) ds. It needs its own discussion:
- what it costs in each regime: in the sampled regime it's a convolution
  on the grid, like the residual prototype; in the functional regime it's
  a quadrature per evaluation point, and the result is not a piecewise
  polynomial;
- whether it is offered for VIDE, and what "iterated" means for VIE-1;
- what the API looks like (a method on `VolterraSolution`, or a solver
  option);
- whether it changes the `at_breakpoints` default.

The design below leaves room for it as an addition.

*Measured 2026-10-31* (brute-force quadrature on today's dense output; K = e⁻ᵘ,
y = cos t on [0,4], m = 3, M = 8→32; scratchpad `iterated_orders.py`,
`iterated_split.py`):

| Method | uₕ uniform | u_it uniform | u_it at mesh points |
|---|---|---|---|
| VIE-2 Gauss | 3 | 4 | ≥ 6 (reaches 1e-15 by M = 32) |
| VIE-2 Radau IIA | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| VIE-2 {0,1/2,1} (default) | 3 | 4 | 4 (= uₕ there) |
| VIE-2 {1/3,2/3,1} | 3 | 3 | — |
| VIDE Gauss | 4 | 6 | 6 |
| VIDE {0,1/2,1} (default) | 4 | 4 | — |

VIE-2: one extra order uniformly when κ ≥ 1, and order m+κ at mesh points.
VIDE with Gauss nodes: 2m uniformly. The rational node sets of the sampled
regime gain at most one order.

*Decided 2026-10-31:* the iterated solution comes **after 1.0**: functional
regime, VIE-2 and VIDE, as an additive `iterated=` keyword. The name is
reserved in the contract (§7), and the `"mean"` default stays.

---

## 3. Target public surface (0.11 additions; all that remains in 1.0)

```python notest
solve_vie1(*, kernel, g=None, continuous=False, y0=None,
           dt=1.0, coll_setting=None, quadrature="product",
           samples_per_interval=None, kernel_interp_degree=None,      # sampled
           mesh=None, coll_nodes=None,
           kernel_singularity=None, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True        # functional
           ) -> VolterraSolution

solve_vie2(*, kernel, g=None,
           dt=1.0, coll_setting=None, quadrature="product",
           samples_per_interval=None, kernel_interp_degree=None,
           mesh=None, coll_nodes=None,
           kernel_singularity=None, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True) -> VolterraSolution

solve_vide(*, kernel, a=None, g=None, y0,
           dt=1.0, coll_setting=None, quadrature="product",
           samples_per_interval=None, kernel_interp_degree=None,
           mesh=None, coll_nodes=None,
           kernel_singularity=None, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True) -> VolterraSolution

VolesWarning, AccuracyWarning, PerformanceWarning
optimal_graded_mesh(*, alpha, t_end, n_intervals, order)
gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes, lobatto_nodes
__version__

docs.title: VolterraSolution
docs.text:
Below, shape is () (scalar), (d,) (vector) or (d, m) (matrix). The dtype is complex for complex inputs.

Grid output. Each attribute means the same thing in both regimes.

Attribute Shape Sampled Functional t (K,) n·dt, K = N (computed on first access) mesh breakpoints, K = M+1 y (K, *shape) values from D, as today the mesh values, evaluated

Interior breakpoints use the mean convention. y is writable (users subtract exact solutions in place). Invariant: sol(sol.t) equals sol.y to rounding.

Piecewise-polynomial structure. Identical in both regimes; read-only unless noted.

Attribute Shape Meaning mesh (M+1,) breakpoints node_times (M, p) the actual collocation times, stored: on the sampled regime's final interval (Q+r samples) the nodes are snapped to that interval's own grid, so they can't be derived from mesh and nodes node_values (M, p, *shape) the collocation values (the unknowns). Functional: the solve output. Sampled: computed lazily from coefficients. Equals the old callable-family return. coefficients (M, P, *shape) local monomial coefficients in x = (t − tₙ)/hₙ ∈ [0,1]. This is the public accessor the noisy-data residual helper needs. nodes (p,) nominal node positions as floats coll_setting — (divs, [choices]) in the sampled regime, None in the functional regime equation — "vie1", "vie2" or "vide" regime — "sampled" or "functional" continuous — whether the space is C⁰: VIDE, or VIE-1 with continuous=True

Evaluation. - __call__(t, *, at_breakpoints="mean") returns (len(t), *shape), and a scalar t gives a scalar or a shape array (F20, documented). It returns NaN outside [0, T] (F21, documented). - at_breakpoints ∈ {"mean", "left", "right"} and only affects interior breakpoints. - Breakpoints are detected within a few ulps, because n·dt and n·(Q·dt) can differ by one ulp and exact equality would silently fall back to one limit. - At t = 0 only the right limit exists; at t = T only the left. - to_ppoly() returns a scipy.interpolate.PPoly: coefficients cₖ/hₙᵏ, highest degree first, trailing axes shape. That gives derivatives, antiderivatives, integrals and roots. PPoly evaluates right-continuously, and the docstring says so. Complex coefficients must be verified before promising them; if PPoly can't take them, raise TypeError for complex solutions. - __repr__ shows the equation, regime, interval count, T, degree, node set, shape and dtype. - Pickling works; lazy caches are not pickled. Pickles are not promised stable across minor versions; the stability policy says so. - No __len__, indexing, iteration, .polynomials, mesh_breakpoints or from_unit_coefs. These are deprecated aliases in 0.11 only.

Efficiency rules: - Nothing on the default path gets more expensive than today. In the sampled regime y comes from D unchanged. node_values and t are computed on first access. - Dense evaluation: a Horner loop indexing one coefficient at a time (c[idx, k]) instead of today's self._unit[idx] copy. That copy is (len(t), P, *shape), hundreds of MB for a matrix solution on a fine grid. The arithmetic order is unchanged, so the result is bitwise identical. - Coefficients are always produced. The D calls currently skip them when return_polys=False; Phase 7 measures the cost of always asking. I expect it to be negligible, since they are about N·p/Q, versus N for y. - Lazy caches are filled without a lock. That's a benign race, because the computations are idempotent.

docs.title: Shape and matrix-mode rule (F11, F19), stated once
docs.text:
• The time axis comes first.
  • The solution is matrix-valued exactly when some input has a column axis: sampled g (N,d,m), callable g returning (d,m), or y0 (d,m).
  • Every input with a column axis must have the same m.
  • An input without one is shared across all columns. This generalises VIDE's shared-(N,d) forcing to all solvers.
  • Complex inputs give complex outputs, and float32 is upcast.
  • A 2-D kernel array is rejected, which keeps it free for a future non-convolution K(tᵢ, sⱼ) (F25).

docs.title: Kernel convention (F25)
docs.text: A callable kernel is called with one positional array argument u and means K(t − s). A future non-convolution kernel will get a new keyword, never arity sniffing (which breaks on functools.partial, np.vectorize and numba dispatchers). Adding a keyword is non-breaking, so 1.0 only has to not promise arity-based dispatch.

docs.title: 4. Phases
docs.text: Each phase leaves pytest tests/ green, passes the bitwise battery (§5), and ends with an offer to commit. Phases 1–3 change no public signature.

docs.title: Phase 0: contract and baseline
docs.text:
1. Write the contract doc (docs/dev/api-contract-1.0.md; it becomes the user-facing conventions page in Phase 6). It covers:
  2. the regime rule
  3. the shape and matrix rule
  4. the breakpoint convention
  5. the kernel convention and reserved extensions
  6. the type/value error policy (F3: wrong type → TypeError, right type with a wrong value → ValueError; ints are numbers.Integral and not bool; bools must be bool/np.bool_)
  7. the warnings policy
  8. non-finite handling
  9. RuntimeError meaning "internal error, please report" (F4)
  10. the stability policy draft (F31)
  11. Baseline battery: generalise docs/dev/nogc_battery.py into docs/dev/api_battery.py, extended with:
  12. every old-API parameter combination (both families, all three solvers, scalar/vector/runtime-d/matrix/complex, both quadratures, continuous VIE-1, graded meshes, kernel_singularity forms, coll_nodes, a short final interval)

Save the reference from main before Phase 1. compare requires exact equality. 3. Benchmark baseline: run benchmarks/bench_solvers.py locally and keep the JSON. Small-N cases matter here, since the new validation layer is pure overhead there.

docs.title: Phase 1: foundations (no signature changes)
docs.text:
1. _warnings.py: the three classes and _warn(msg, category).
  2. stacklevel is computed by walking frames to the first non-voles frame. That's needed for Python 3.10/3.11; skip_file_prefixes only arrived in 3.12.
  3. Convert all 15 print sites (F1).
  4. show_warnings=False becomes an internal suppress flag checked inside _warn, not warnings.catch_warnings: that mutates process-global state and isn't thread-safe before 3.14, and the matrix path fans out to threads.
  5. The per-column recursive calls (e.g. _col_vie1 → solve_VIE_1 near solvers.py:1299) already pass show_warnings=False. Audit them so every warning is emitted once, from the calling thread (F2).
  6. _validate.py: one helper per parameter kind (integer, positive integer, bool, positive finite real, choice, 1-D increasing finite array starting at 0, array or callable, coll setting, …), each applying the F3 rule. Route _as_int, _check_time_step and friends through it. Behaviour changes, all for the changelog:
  7. coll_divs=2.0 raises TypeError
  8. time_step="0.1" raises a voles TypeError instead of the > comparison error
  9. show_warnings="no" and return_function=1 raise TypeError
  10. Phase 0 bug (a): _resolve_node_pos validates coll_divs as a positive integer (TypeError for 2.5 or 2.0), like the array family's _as_int. F5: soln_init_value=None on VIDE (both families) raises TypeError ("y0 is required").
  11. F4: _dlang.py:246 raises RuntimeError("internal error: <fn> returned code n; please report at <issues URL>"), listed in the Raises sections. Codes 1 (argument checks that Python already enforces) and 3 (too large, already a ValueError) are the only nonzero returns today.
  12. F6: the finite checks of D12.
  13. F17: move _smooth_gl_order to a module constant (_SMOOTH_GL_ORDER); only src/ uses it.
  14. F24: quadrature accepted case-insensitively.
  15. pytest: set filterwarnings = ["error"] plus explicit ignores, so every warning site must be expected with pytest.warns. Rewrite test_show_warnings.py from capsys to pytest.warns / recwarn, and add a test that a suppressed solve emits nothing from any thread.

Battery: numerics bitwise equal. The expected-exception table is updated only for the deliberate F3/F5 changes, each listed in the commit message.

docs.title: Phase 2: VolterraSolution
docs.text:
1. Build VolterraSolution (§3) in _solution.py from today's _SolutionFunction, plus:
  2. the grid output (t, y)
  3. node_times, node_values and the metadata
  4. at_breakpoints with tolerant breakpoint detection
  5. the copy-free Horner loop
  6. to_ppoly(), with complex support verified or refused explicitly
  7. __repr__
  8. 0.11-only deprecated aliases: mesh_breakpoints, polynomials (_polys_from_unit_coefs moves behind it), __getitem__, __iter__, __len__. Keep the legacy _SolutionFunction class unchanged in 0.11 so 0.10 pickles still load; delete it in 1.0.
  9. Internal constructor: VolterraSolution._build(raw, regime, equation, …) takes the cores' _Raw (Phase 3). Until Phase 3 lands, an adapter builds it from today's (values, _SolutionFunction) output.
  10. Tests:
  11. the invariant sol(sol.t) == sol.y (to rounding), in both regimes, for continuous and discontinuous methods
  12. the left/right/mean limits against direct polynomial evaluation
  13. breakpoint detection with ulp-perturbed t
  14. NaN outside [0, T]
  15. to_ppoly() against sol(t) away from breakpoints, plus its .derivative() against differentiated coefficients
  16. read-only flags; repr; a pickle round-trip
